verdict: Where this syllabus is Swedish it is genuinely good – är as a single copula, den/det här with the doubled definite, sin/sitt, ju/väl/nog, halv tre counting forward, spår not plattform, ligger vs är, lagom, tvättstugan, hekto, vabba, leg, the du-reform framing: these are things a real Swedish course teaches and a Hindi port would never have found. The defects are structural, not lexical. First, the Hindi spine is still visible in roughly fifty learner-facing notes: Devanagari sits in five of them (hs-0002, hs-0046, hs-0062, hs-0123, hs-0127), sixteen say "substituted for biryani / the sari / the rickshaw / achaar / WhatsApp", thirteen say "re-tiered up/down" (authoring metadata leaking into the card), and eleven separate N/A slots plus three more about är all restate that Swedish lacks honorifics and person agreement – close to four percent of the syllabus spent describing the absence of Hindi rather than the presence of Swedish. Second, duplication is severe: I counted sixty-plus repeats (köttbullar, kanelbulle, tunnelbana, alltså, ledig and mig all appear three times; midsommar, vi ses, lätt, dem, element, kök, bröd, smör, väg, familj, mamma, pappa, svärmor and dozens more twice), several at conflicting tiers, so the real teachable count is nearer 1,050. Third, the two rules that actually build Swedish sentences – main-clause V2 and subordinate-clause inte-fronting – exist only as asides inside other items' notes, while hålla på att gets three separate entries; the -s verbs (ses, hörs, träffas, finns, känns) are scattered as vocabulary with no paradigm explaining them, and reflexives and compounding are untaught as systems. Fourth, one tier-1 paradigm is factually wrong: hs-0030 states "infinitive + -r", which yields köpar and sovar. Fifth, the whole social-drinking layer is missing – no öl, no vin, no Systembolaget, no skål – and so are tack för maten and tack för senast, the two most near-obligatory formulas in a Swedish friend's home; also absent are snö, mörkt, grader, frukost, kvitto, plånbok, personnummer, dricks and "hur kommer jag till...?". Sixth, gender is marked on maybe a quarter of nouns even though the syllabus twice tells the learner to learn every noun with its en/ett. Finally, register is inverted at the very top: "ett ögonblick" and "jag skulle vilja ha" sit at tier 1 above "kan jag få", weekdays sit at 3 while söndag sits at 2, and months at 4. Fix the leakage sweep, dedupe, add V2/bisats, and this is a strong course.

items.note: One form for every person: jag är, du är, vi är. Swedish verbs never agree with the subject.
Two different words: nej is the standalone 'no', inte is 'not' (hs-0233). To contradict a negative question you need jo.
To contradict a negative question say jo, not ja: 'Kommer du inte?' – 'Jo!'
Said 'ja(g)' – the g is normally silent.
The du-reform of the 1960s killed polite address. Du to your boss, your doctor and strangers alike.
Said 'va'. On its own, 'Va?' is the everyday 'sorry, what?'
den här before en-words, det här before ett-words, and the noun stays definite: den här bilen.
Things take den (en-words) or det (ett-words). They = de, always said 'dom', as is dem.
No apostrophe. For 'of' with things use a compound or av: husets tak, taket på huset.
i for inside; på for 'on' and for a surprising number of places (på jobbet, på bussen, på toa).
Direction and recipient: jag går till stan, jag ger den till Anna. Swedish has no object marker – word order does that job.
Origin and source: 'jag kommer från England'. ifrån is the emphatic form that shows up in 'var kommer du ifrån?'
The workhorse preposition: på bordet, på jobbet, på svenska, på fredag.
Said 'ock' or just 'å'.
Starting a sentence with så pushes the verb to second place: 'Så gick vi hem.' That verb-second rule runs through all of Swedish.
Plural only in modern Swedish. Aimed at one person it sounds stiff, old-fashioned or faintly sarcastic.
Works at any hour with anyone. Doubled up, 'hej hej', it can also mean bye.
The everyday yes to a suggestion. 'Det är bra' does the same job.
Never changes form. As a reaction, 'jaha' is the 'oh, I see'.
Said 'okso'. Sits after the verb: 'Jag tycker också om det.' Spoken shortcut: 'jag med' = me too.
gör / gjorde / gjort. Said with a soft 'y' start: 'yöra'.
är / var / varit. 'To happen' is hända.
gå is on foot. Going anywhere by vehicle is åka (hs-0081) – saying 'jag går till Malmö' means you are walking there.
kommer / kom / kommit.

items.word: jag pratar / du pratar / vi pratar
items.roman: jag pratar / du pratar / vi pratar
items.en: present tense: one form for every person – pratar, köper, skriver, bor
items.note: The ending is a property of the verb: -ar (prata → pratar), -er (köpa → köper, skriva → skriver) or bare -r (bo → bor). One present covers both 'I speak' and 'I'm speaking' – Swedish has no continuous tense.
min before en-words, mitt before ett-words, mina before plurals: min bil, mitt hus, mina barn.
din / ditt / dina, same pattern as min.
Said 'mej', and often written that way in texts.
Said 'dej'.
var for standing still, vart for movement: 'Var är du?' but 'Vart ska du?'
mycket for uncountables, många for countables: hur många biljetter?
där is static, dit is movement: 'Jag ska dit imorgon.'
'nyss' is 'a moment ago'; 'strax' is 'in a moment'.
Both are two words underneath: i morgon, i går. Don't mix up i morgon (tomorrow) with på morgonen (in the morning).
Spoken form of sedan. 'Igen' is 'again' (hs-0206).
Said 'mycke'. Before adjectives spoken Swedish prefers the prefix jätte-: jättebra, jättetrött, jättegott.
'lite grann' = just a tiny bit.
'för mycket' = too much.
'få' = few, 'för lite' = too little.
What you say when someone is pouring or serving: 'tack, det räcker'.
alla for people and countables, allt for stuff in general (hs-0271).
Everyone says and texts nåt.
Said nån. Plural några, said nåra.
'Folk säger så' = people say that. människor is the countable, slightly more formal word.
Very spoken: 'det är ingen stor grej' = it's no big deal. sak is the neutral word (hs-0066).
ett jobb. jobba = to work; arbete/arbeta are the formal pair.
ett hem. hus is a house as a building. hem = (to) home, hemma = at home: 'jag åker hem' vs 'jag är hemma'.
ett namn. But to say your name you use heter, not namn (hs-0101).
Tap water is excellent and free – asking for kranvatten in a café is completely normal.
ett kaffe. Offered constantly, and refusing twice is fine. te exists, but coffee is the social default.
äta = to eat (äter / åt / ätit).
Always plural. Cash is nearly extinct – 'kan jag swisha?' is the everyday question.
'Har du tid?' = have you got a minute? 'en tid' also means an appointment.
'ett bra ställe' = a good spot. plats is a seat or a space.
ger / gav / gett. Said with a soft 'y': 'ye'.
tar / tog / tagit.
ser / såg / sett. 'titta på' = to watch.
hör / hörde / hört. 'lyssna på' = to listen to.
The spoken default. tala is formal and sounds like a news reader.
säger (said 'säjer') / sa / sagt.
'ska vi träffas?' = shall we meet up? 'få' is to get.
vet / visste / vetat. Knowing a person is känna, knowing how to do something is kunna.
Lives mostly in 'ingen aning' = no idea (hs-0188).
förstår / förstod / förstått. 'fatta' is the everyday spoken version.
bor / bodde / bott. 'stanna' is to stay put or to stop.
vill + a verb (jag vill åka), but vill HA + a thing (jag vill ha kaffe). behöver = need.
dricker / drack / druckit.

items.en: to go by vehicle; to travel
items.note: åka buss, åka tåg, åka till Göteborg. Swedish insists on the difference between åka and gå (on foot).

items.en: to fix; laga mat = to cook
items.note: 'making' in general is göra (hs-0026).
Swedish picks the verb by posture: lägga (flat), ställa (upright), sätta (set in place). behålla = to keep.

items.en: imperative = the bare verb stem; there are no politeness levels
items.note: Politeness comes from rephrasing as 'kan du...?' or adding tack, not from the verb form.
For 'right, let's go' Swedes say 'ska vi gå?' or, casually, 'då drar vi'.
At the door: 'kom in, kom in!' Shoes come off in the hall, always.
Literally 'strike yourself down'. 'sätt dig' is blunter, fine among friends.
Also the reply to tack, and 'go ahead'. Plural varsågoda when addressing a table.
'Berätta!' invites the whole story.
Gets attention and apologises for small things. förlåt is a real apology (hs-0091).
A genuine apology. 'Förlåt?' with a rising tone also means 'sorry, what?'
Swedish has no everyday 'please'. You tack at the end of a request – 'en kaffe, tack' – or ask with 'kan du...?'. snälla is for begging.
Also 'det är lugnt' (very spoken) and 'det gör inget'.
tack is what turns a bare ja or nej into a civil answer to an offer.
The light greeting. 'hur mår du?' (hs-0348) is a real question about your health, so save it.
'helt okej' and 'det rullar på' are the modest alternatives.
'vad har hänt?' for something just now.
Literally 'I am called'. 'mitt namn är' sounds like filling in a form.
'jag är sugen på nåt' = I fancy something.
måste takes a bare infinitive, no att. 'jag måste dra' is the casual 'I've got to run'.
Tagged on the end, 'eller?' turns a statement into a question: 'Det är bra, eller?'
Often just för in speech. After it the clause reorders: inte goes before the verb – 'för att jag inte kan'.
aj for pain, usch for yuck, hallå to get someone's attention.
The gender split that runs through everything: en bil, ett hus. Learn every noun together with its en or ett.
Yes, the same word as the other sex. Nobody blinks.
The famous sj-sound: a breathy 'hw' from the back of the mouth.
Said 'nie'.
Said 'tie'.
Plural bröder. 'brorsa' is the slangy one.
Plural systrar. 'syrra' is the slangy one.
sonen, söner. Never used to address anyone – Swedes use first names.
dottern, döttrar.
The Swedish gesture of care. Asking whether someone has eaten is not a greeting here; offering fika is.
kan + a language, no verb needed.
A bare 'va?' is the normal quick version; 'förlåt?' is politer.
'jag förstår' is the neutral one; 'ah, okej' does most of the work in practice.

items.en: how do you say that in Swedish?

items.note: Languages are lower case. 'på svenska' = in Swedish.
'för dig' = for you. Purpose before a verb is 'för att' + infinitive.
Also 'by' for transport: åka med bussen. 'hänger du med?' = are you coming along?
har / hade / haft. Also the auxiliary for the perfect: 'jag har ätit'.
kan / kunde / kunnat, and kan takes a bare infinitive: jag kan simma.
'fort' and 'snabbt' are quickly; 'skynda dig' is hurry up.
'klockan tre' = at three. In speech it often drops away: 'vi ses tre'.
The spoken default. vän is warmer and weightier – you have few of those.
What people actually say; pojke is textbook. 'min kille' = my boyfriend.
Said 'shay'. 'min tjej' = my girlfriend. flicka sounds childish or official.
Also the impersonal 'one/you': 'man säger så här' = you say it like this. Hugely common.
In casual talk people say 'en tjej' for any youngish woman.
A particle verb, and the particle carries the stress: ta MED. Swedish builds meaning this way constantly.
'öppet' = open (of a shop): 'har ni öppet?'
stänga = to close, stänga av = to switch off, sätta på = to switch on.
telefon sounds like a landline or an official form.
Swedes usually answer by saying their own name instead. hallå is for 'are you still there?' and for calling out.
ringer / ringde / ringt, and no preposition: jag ringer dig.
prata med a person, prata om a subject.
knäckebröd is the crispbread on every table; a sandwich is 'en macka'.
Less central than most learners expect – potatis and pasta are the everyday sides.
The homely default plate: köttbullar with potatis, gräddsås and lingonsylt.
Said 'myölk'. Ordered by fat: standard, mellan, lätt.
'är det starkt?' Rarely needed with Swedish food, but useful at a kebab or Thai place.
Also a verb: 'ska vi fika?' Coffee plus something sweet, and it is an invitation to sit down. The core social ritual, at work and at home.
The offer itself is 'vill du ha mer?'
gott is tasty; 'bra mat' only means decent food. Say it and you have made a friend.
ett rum, rummet, and the plural is unchanged: två rum.
Short for toalett, and what everyone says. badrum is the bathroom at home.
Informally 'spänn': hundra spänn. Card or Swish everywhere; cash is close to extinct.
Haggling is not a thing – the price is the price.
'vänta lite' = hang on a sec. stanna is to stop moving.
stor / stort / stora, by gender and number.
Wildly irregular: liten (en), litet (ett), lilla (the definite), små (plural).
Said 'kanshe'. Unusually, it does not force inversion in speech: 'Han kanske kommer'.
Stress the om. 'gilla' (hs-0186) is the more casual everyday verb.
Swedish softens with tiny unstressed words – nog, väl, ju, då: 'det går nog bra', 'kom då!'
Said 'sverje'. A Swede is 'en svensk', the adjective is svensk.
Almost everyone speaks it well – 'kan vi ta det på engelska?' always works, which is exactly why you have to push yourself.
bagage or väskor for luggage.

items.word: jag är / du är / vi är / de är
items.roman: jag ar / du ar / vi ar / de ar
items.en: present of vara: är for every person
items.note: Past var, supine varit. The whole verb system works this way – one form per tense.
Also written ok. 'visst' is the warmer version.
The single most useful word in Swedish. It ends requests ('en kaffe, tack') and answers offers ('ja tack').
What a host says at the table. 'smaklig måltid' is the restaurant-ish 'enjoy your meal'.
'kan jag få ..., tack' is shorter and just as polite – the everyday way to order.
'jag gillar det' is what people say; tycka om is the neutral written pair.
'jag vet inte' is the plain version.
lära sig is reflexive: jag lär mig, du lär dig. And the plain present covers 'am learning'.
No do-support: a yes/no question is just the verb first, then the subject.
'jag är från Storbritannien' for the UK; a Brit is 'en britt'.
ligger for places and buildings, är for objects you have mislaid.
'Hej, det är Tom.' Swedes announce themselves rather than saying hello.
Spoken: 'vänta lite' or 'en sekund'.
In a real emergency shout 'hjälp!' and ring 112.
'vi ses' = see you; 'ha det bra' = take care.
'sköt om dig' is warmer, for someone who is unwell or going through it.
The standard offer on arrival; 'ska vi ta en fika?' invites the whole ritual.
ett barn, barnet, and the plural is barn – no ending. Definite plural barnen.
The staple. potatismos is mash.

items.en: one 'you' for everyone; ni is plural only
items.note: Sweden abolished polite address in the du-reform. There is no ladder to climb – say du to the prime minister.
Casual. 'tusen tack' is thanks a million.
Also 'what's wrong?' when someone looks off.
Often clipped to 'eller hu'. A tagged-on 'va?' does the same job in speech.
Swedish food is not spicy, so the useful version of this request is dietary: 'utan lök, tack', 'jag är allergisk mot nötter'.
Said 'yelp'.
Pairs with farsan for dad. Blunt but affectionate, and only about your own parents.
Swedish uses the adjective, not a noun: 'jag är hungrig', never 'I have hunger'. 'sugen' = peckish.
'har du...?' for do you have. For 'there is' use det finns (hs-0215).
finns is existence, är is identity: 'det finns ingen mjölk' vs 'mjölken är sur'. English speakers get this wrong for months.
Pointing in a shop: 'den där, tack'. den där for en-words, det där for ett-words.
Swedes open with du plus the name: 'Du, Anna – har du tid?' For a stranger, ursäkta.
Said 'å'. Both 'jag tror att han kommer' and 'jag börjar att förstå'. In a clause after att, inte moves in front of the verb.
Tagged on the end: 'det är kallt, va?' The full form is eller hur.

items.en: to be in the middle of doing
items.note: 'jag håller på att laga mat'. Swedish has no continuous tense – normally the plain present covers it, so this is for stressing the ongoing bit.

items.en: past of vara: var for every person
items.note: Supine varit, used with har: 'jag har varit i Malmö'.
Never change form for the noun. But when the owner is the sentence's own subject you need sin/sitt instead (hs-0243).
vår / vårt / våra.
Spoken: 'vad för nåt?' = what sort of thing?
Agrees: vilken buss, vilket tåg, vilka biljetter.
dagen, dagar. 'om dagen' = per day.
berätta FÖR someone about something. 'säga till' = to let someone know.
fråga is to ask a question; 'be om' is to ask for a thing.
'det verkar bra'. For feeling use känns ('det känns konstigt'), for duration use tar ('det tar en timme').
sover / sov / sovit.
sitta is the state, 'sätta sig' is the act of sitting down.
'vakna' is to wake up; 'stiga upp' is the formal get up.
Comes after the verb in a main clause ('jag vet inte') but before it in a subordinate clause ('...att jag inte vet'). Negative commands: 'gör inte det'.
The all-purpose way to ask for anything, in a shop, a bar or a friend's kitchen. Add tack.
The natural follow-on after ursäkta when stopping a stranger.
'tusen tack' is warmer, 'stort tack' is for writing.
Spoken: 'allt väl?' or 'är det lugnt?'
Very casual, from 'hur är läget?'. Answer 'bra' or 'det rullar på'.
Also 'whether': 'jag vet inte om han kommer'.
Said 'asså' and used constantly as a filler. Its partner in crime is 'typ' (like, sort of).
Unstressed, never first in the sentence: 'det är ju sant' = well, it IS true. Using it right is the fastest way to sound Swedish.

items.en: his/her/their own, pointing back at the subject
items.note: 'Han tog sin jacka' = his own coat. 'Han tog hans jacka' = someone else's. Swedish keeps this distinction rigidly.

items.word: en stor bil / ett stort hus / stora bilar / den stora bilen
items.roman: en stor bil / ett stort hus / stora bilar / den stora bilen
items.en: adjective agreement: -Ø with en-words, -t with ett-words, -a in the plural and after the/this/my
items.note: The definite form takes both a front word and the -a: den stora bilen.
'vi hörs' if you will be in touch by phone or message instead.
tills before a clause, till before a point in time: 'till fredag', 'tills du kommer'.

items.word: prata → pratade / köpa → köpte / skriva → skrev
items.roman: prata → pratade / kopa → kopte / skriva → skrev
items.en: past tense: weak verbs add -ade/-de/-te, strong verbs change the vowel
items.note: Same form for every person. The weak classes are predictable; the strong verbs (skriva/skrev, dricka/drack) have to be learned one by one.
Present tense plus a time word does most of the work in speech: 'jag åker imorgon'.

items.word: bil → bilen; ett hus → huset; bilar → bilarna
items.roman: bil → bilen; ett hus → huset; bilar → bilarna
items.en: 'the' is a suffix stuck on the end of the noun
items.note: The first real hurdle in Swedish: 'the' is glued on the end. en-words take -en, ett-words -et, plurals -na/-en.

items.en: offers and permission: shall we / may I
items.note: 'ska vi gå?' = shall we go. 'får jag...?' = may I. 'kan du...?' = could you.
'den i blått' = the one in blue. For doer nouns Swedish adds -are: bagare, lärare.
Comparatives add -are: billigare än, större än.
billigast, störst; long adjectives take mest (mest intressant). bäst and sämst are irregular.
'det är klart' = it's ready. 'klart!' on its own = of course.
tycker is an opinion, tror is a guess or a belief, tänker is what is going on in your head.
What people actually say when leaving is 'jag måste nog dra'.
Tap water is free and asking for it is completely normal.
först = first of all; innan and före = before.
'vi hörs senare'. 'strax' = in a moment.
'efteråt' = afterwards.
innan before a clause, före before a noun or time.
'den andra' = the other one; 'en annan' = another one.
'inget' is the short spoken form.
allt for things, alla for people (hs-0053).
'vilken tid?' works too. Answer: 'klockan sju'.
'en halvtimme' = half an hour.
ett år, and the plural is unchanged: tre år.
'i morse' = this morning just gone; förmiddag is the late morning.
'i kväll' = this evening. eftermiddag is the afternoon.
'i natt' covers both tonight and last night; context decides.

items.en: the day after tomorrow / the day before yesterday

items.note: Beware: 'halv tre' means half past TWO. Swedish counts towards the coming hour.
Literally 'my man'. make is formal. 'sambo' – live-in partner – is extremely common and carries no stigma.
As a title fru is dead; only 'min fru' survives. Unmarried couples say sambo or partner.
'hela släkten' = the whole extended family; a släktträff is the family gathering.
barn is the same in the plural, so only the ending marks it: barn, barnen.
'gifta sig' = to get married; 'gift' = married.
tänka is thinking or intending, tycka is having an opinion, tro is believing.
Reflexive: jag lär mig, du lär dig, vi lär oss.
köper / köpte / köpt.
'läsa svenska' = to study Swedish.
skriver / skrev / skrivit.
'skicka ett sms'.
'jag drar nu' is the spoken 'right, I'm off'.
'vi kom fram vid sex'. anlända is timetable Swedish.
hjälpa någon MED något – no preposition before the person.
Often without att in speech: 'jag försöker prata svenska'.
börjar / började / börjat. 'sätta igång' = to get going.
'mjölken är slut' = we're out of milk. 'slutet' = the end.
'jag har glömt' if it is still gone from your head.
'det bryts' = you're breaking up.
Also 'cute' about a person. Of food people usually just say gott.
'ont i magen' = stomach ache.
'proppmätt' = stuffed. Declining more: 'tack, det räcker'.
ett tåg. pendeltåg is the commuter train; SJ runs the long-distance ones.
'T-banan' in speech, and Stockholm only. Elsewhere it is buses and spårvagn (trams).
Bought in an app almost everywhere; you rarely pay a driver.
hållplats = bus stop; spår or perrong = platform.
butik works too; a food shop is a mataffär – ICA, Coop, Willys.
Sweden's shopping happens in supermarkets and köpcentrum; a torg is where the market stalls stand.
gata is a street. 'vilken väg ska jag gå?'
'det är dyrt' about a situation, 'en dyr bil' about a thing.
ny / nytt / nya.
gammal / gammalt / gamla, and used of people too – no offence taken.
'det är varmt ute'. het is reserved for genuinely burning things.
'det är kallt ute'; kylig is chilly.
dålig is bad; 'det funkar inte' is the everyday 'it doesn't work'.
'det stämmer' = that's right, that checks out.
'jag blir glad' = it makes me happy. lycklig is the deep, life-level kind.
'städa' is to clean or tidy up.
'är du klar?' can mean both are you ready and have you finished. färdig is a synonym.
nödvändig is 'strictly necessary'.
'visst!' and 'gärna!' are the warmer yeses.
'precis!' on its own means 'quite so'. 'helt klart' = definitely.
Spoken: 'jaså?', a rising 'va?', or 'seriöst?' among younger people.
'ganska bra' = pretty good. 'rätt så bra' does the same.
Before an adjective, så alone does it: 'så gott!'
Also softens: 'jag ska bara...' = I'll just... (famously the Swedish excuse for another five minutes).
'härligt!' and 'vad trevligt!' do the same job; 'oj!' is surprise.
The standard warm yes to an invitation, and a politeness marker inside requests.
Spoken: 'ingen fara' or 'det löser sig'.
'tack för i kväll' is the fixed thing you say on leaving, and a text the next day is expected.

items.en: what did you think of it?
items.note: About food: 'var det gott?'
Short for gratulerar. 'grattis på födelsedagen' = happy birthday.
'hur mår du?' is literally 'how do you feel'. 'må dåligt' = to feel rough, in body or mind.
A real question, not a greeting – asked when someone has been ill or is having a hard time, and answered honestly.
You never address one as 'doktor'. You ring 1177 for advice and go to vårdcentralen.
apotek is the pharmacy. Paracetamol is Alvedon, and it is on the shelf.
Used as 'ha ont i' + body part: 'jag har ont i huvudet' = my head hurts.
'ta det lugnt' = take it easy.
'vilket väder!' Weather is the safest and most-used small talk there is.
'varmt' covers heat. Summer runs the social calendar: semester (the long holiday) and midsommar.
A cold, the illness, is 'förkylning': 'jag är förkyld'.
'det regnar'. Said 'rängn'.
'på jobbet' = at work. kontor is the office building.
Spoken form of staden: 'vi ses i stan', 'åka in till stan'.
'ute på landet'. by means village but matters far less here – most people head to a stuga.
ett land, landet – the same word that means countryside in 'på landet'.
'jag är ledig imorgon'. semester is annual leave, lov is a school holiday.
'ta en bild'. foto works too.
Always plural. 'ta på dig' = put on, 'ta av dig' = take off, and shoes come off indoors.
er / ert / era, matching ni. There is no familiar/polite split to worry about.
Never changes – but use sin/sitt/sina when it points back at the subject.
Same form as the possessive: 'jag såg er igår'. Singular is dig.
Object forms. Things take den or det; 'them' is dem, said and often written dom.

lunch is early, 11 to 12, and middag is the cooked evening meal around six. kvällsmat is the light bite after.
'Var ligger...?' asks where a place is; this asks how to get there. The one you will use most as a visitor.
'det snöar' = it's snowing. halka is the ice underfoot that follows, and halka omkull is what you then do.
'det blir mörkt vid tre' – the darkness from November to January is the single most-discussed fact of Swedish life. ljust is its opposite.
Temperature is always in grader; below zero people say 'minus fem' or 'fem minusgrader'.

Casual hello, mostly younger people and men. 'tjena, läget?' hej is the safe one with anyone.

Where friends disappear at weekends and for all of July. If you make Swedish friends you will end up in one – 'ute på landet'.
